subtopics.title: Conduction: contact paths, material stacks and thermal leaks
subtopics.learning_goal: Conduction carries energy down a temperature gradient. For specified steady one-dimensional paths, thermal resistances combine in series and independent parallel paths carry separate heat currents.

science_records.claim: Conduction carries energy down a temperature gradient. For specified steady one-dimensional paths, thermal resistances combine in series and independent parallel paths carry separate heat currents.
science_records.law_or_model: P=ΔT/R; R=L/(kA); R_series=ΣR; 1/R_parallel=Σ(1/R), for the stated steady linear conduction model (authored enrichment).
assumptions: Steady linear one-dimensional conduction; k constant over the stated range, no storage or unmodelled side losses.
Series layers share power only at steady state without side paths; parallel paths share endpoint temperatures.
conditions_and_limits: Steady linear one-dimensional conduction; k constant over the stated range, no storage or unmodelled side losses.
Series layers share power only at steady state without side paths; parallel paths share endpoint temperatures.
Contact resistance and radiation/convection require separate accounting where relevant.
Surface sensation is not a direct measurement of temperature or conductivity.
science_records.units_and_signs: P in W, ΔT in K, R in K/W, L in m, k in W/(m K), A in m².

core1a.phenomenon: A small metal fastener can bypass an otherwise effective layer of insulation.
core1a.scientific_narrative:
Heat conduction transfers energy through microscopic interactions in matter. Neighbouring particles exchange energy; in metals mobile electrons can contribute strongly. A solid does not need to flow as a whole to conduct. A conductor transfers energy relatively readily, while an insulator transfers it less readily under comparable geometry and conditions. Neither is a source of cold or heat. At equal temperatures, there is no net conductive heat transfer between bodies in equilibrium.

Touching metal and wood at the same room temperature can feel different because the rate of energy transfer from a warmer hand differs. The sensation also depends on contact, geometry and the material's thermal response, not just its temperature. A thermometer tests the temperature claim; controlled heat-flow measurements test the transfer-rate claim.

For a simple steady one-dimensional slab, with constant thermal conductivity k, thickness L, area A and temperatures fixed on its faces, the rate of heat flow is P=kAΔT/L. This quantitative relation is supplied here as enrichment, not a claim that it is compulsory NSEJS content. Define thermal resistance R=L/(kA); the temperature drop across the slab is PR. This resembles a flow-resistance model but concerns energy per time, not material current. The temperature drop is not heat stored in the slab. Doubling thickness doubles resistance under fixed k and A; doubling area halves it.

If layers lie one after another along the same path and there is no storage or side loss at their junction, the steady power through each is equal. Their temperature drops add, so R_total=R₁+R₂. A contact interface can add resistance even when its thickness is negligible; do not assume perfect thermal contact unless stated. If two independent paths connect the same hot and cold surfaces, each experiences the same endpoint temperature difference. Their powers add: P_total=ΔT/R₁+ΔT/R₂. An insulating wall with a metal bolt can therefore lose substantial energy through a small bypass. A low-resistance parallel route does not simply add to the series resistance of the insulating layers.

For a heat-loss investigation, compare the same boundary temperatures, area, contact pressure and steady-state condition. If a sample is still warming, the input power need not equal the transmitted conductive power. Radiation and convection can provide other paths. A model fitted to two conditions is not validated merely because it reproduces those conditions; an unused change of geometry or temperature can test the model. Inverse tasks may have several possible combinations of material/contact/bypass resistances. Identify the additional observation that would distinguish them before claiming a material property. No matching conduction question has been established in the inspectable Core2 bank; the constructions here are authored transfer.

derivation_steps.action: Draw hot and cold boundaries and every physical connection.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Conduction is driven by a temperature difference, and geometry determines which paths exist.

derivation_steps.action: For a series branch, add temperature drops at common power.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Steady conservation with no side losses gives the same power through sequential layers.

derivation_steps.action: For parallel branches, calculate separate powers at the common boundary temperature difference.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Energy transfer rates add at the hot boundary; a bypass can dominate.

derivation_steps.action: Test the model with an independent change or internal temperature observation.
derivation_steps.why_valid: One total resistance alone does not identify all individual resistances.

model_limits: Steady linear one-dimensional conduction; k constant over the stated range, no storage or unmodelled side losses.
Series layers share power only at steady state without side paths; parallel paths share endpoint temperatures.
Contact resistance and radiation/convection require separate accounting where relevant.
Surface sensation is not a direct measurement of temperature or conductivity.

progressive_examples.problem: Two equal-area slabs of the same material differ only in thickness: 2 cm and 4 cm. Compare steady power at the same face temperatures.
progressive_examples.reasoning: The thicker slab has twice the resistance and half the power.

progressive_examples.problem: Two layers R=2 and 3 K/W are in series across 20 K. Find power and temperature drops.
progressive_examples.reasoning: R_total=5 K/W, P=4 W; drops 8 K and 12 K.

progressive_examples.problem: A 5 K/W insulation path and a 10 K/W bolt path share 30 K. Find total loss and what happens if the bolt is removed.
progressive_examples.reasoning: P_ins=6 W, P_bolt=3 W, total 9 W; removing bolt leaves 6 W if conditions unchanged.
progressive_examples.independent_check: Effective R=30/9=3.333 K/W, less than either branch.

figures.scene_description: Two slabs lie on one heat path; the lower fastener connects the same hot and cold boundaries independently. Original inline SVG.

misconception.wrong_model: All resistances always add, and metal feeling colder proves lower temperature.
misconception.diagnostic: Does a bolt lie along the insulation path or connect the same boundaries independently? What would a thermometer show?
misconception.repair: Draw actual paths before combining resistances; check boundary temperatures independently.

exit_check.task: Two series resistances 4 and 2 K/W connect 30 °C to 12 °C. An independent 9 K/W bypass spans the same boundaries. Find total power.

core1b.fresh_task: Two boxes have identical thick insulating walls. Only box A has metal screws joining its inner and outer skins. A technician says both must lose heat at the same rate because wall thicknesses match. Explain a competing prediction and test it.
core1b.protected_work: Explain an unexpected insulation result by identifying the actual energy-transfer paths and separating temperature from conductive rate.

stages.predict: Predict whether matching insulation thickness is enough to make both boxes lose heat equally. State your initial reason.
stages.attempt: Two boxes have identical thick insulating walls. Only box A has metal screws joining its inner and outer skins. A technician says both must lose heat at the same rate because wall thicknesses match. Explain a competing prediction and test it.
stages.reconstruct: Screws supply parallel conducting routes in A, so greater loss is possible despite same main wall; replace or thermally interrupt screws, match boundary temperatures and measure steady input.
stages.diagnose: Identify whether your explanation assumes a material label alone determines the whole rate, or confuses a temperature observation with transfer.
stages.repair: Trace the complete contact path and temperature difference; specify an independent matched measurement before attributing the result.
stages.boundary_test: If the screws touch only the outer skin, does the same bypass explanation necessarily apply?

core1b.fresh_task: Two rods of metal and wood have been in one room for hours. A warm hand touches each; metal feels colder. Later the rods connect the same warm and cold reservoirs. Explain why the two observations need not contradict equal initial temperatures, and identify a measurement of each claim.
core1b.protected_work: Explain an unexpected insulation result by identifying the actual energy-transfer paths and separating temperature from conductive rate.

stages.predict: Do you initially expect the two rods to have different temperatures, different heat-transfer rates, or both? Explain your initial judgement.
stages.attempt: Two rods of metal and wood have been in one room for hours. A warm hand touches each; metal feels colder. Later the rods connect the same warm and cold reservoirs. Explain why the two observations need not contradict equal initial temperatures, and identify a measurement of each claim.
stages.reconstruct: Different contact energy-transfer rates can cause sensation at equal T; thermometer checks T, matched geometry and boundary-temperature steady power compares conduction. Touch alone cannot establish conductivity.
stages.diagnose: Identify whether your explanation assumes a material label alone determines the whole rate, or confuses a temperature observation with transfer.
stages.repair: Trace the complete contact path and temperature difference; specify an independent matched measurement before attributing the result.
stages.boundary_test: If contact resistance differs strongly between the rods and reservoirs, can the measured rates be attributed solely to rod material?

stages.predict: Before drawing, predict whether the metal path changes the power through the main two layers under fixed face temperatures.
stages.attempt: A wall has hot-side 2 K/W and cold-side 4 K/W layers plus a separate 12 K/W metal path. Faces 42 and 18 °C. Draw physical and resistance diagrams, label the junction temperature and each power.
stages.reconstruct: Main branch 4 W; junction 34 °C; bypass 2 W; total 6 W. Endpoints common, no junction on bypass.
stages.diagnose: Check each branch's endpoints and whether the internal temperature drop follows the layer order. Did you put the bridge in series?
stages.repair: Redraw the two routes, calculate branch powers at their common ΔT, then check the main branch junction by adding its drops.
stages.boundary_test: If the metal path is severed without changing boundary temperatures, what changes on each branch?

core1b.fresh_task: At ΔT=30 K, a wall with nominal layer R=5 K/W loses 9 W. Model A says effective layer R scales with thickness but differs from nominal; model B keeps nominal layer and adds a fixed independent bypass. Triple the layer thickness: measured loss 5 W. Determine which model fits and predict loss with doubled thickness.
core1b.protected_work: Discriminate a changed effective slab resistance from a fixed independent bypass using a changed-thickness experiment and an independent prediction.

stages.predict: Predict whether the tripled-thickness observation can distinguish the two proposed explanations. State an initial judgement.
stages.attempt: At ΔT=30 K, a wall with nominal layer R=5 K/W loses 9 W. Model A says effective layer R scales with thickness but differs from nominal; model B keeps nominal layer and adds a fixed independent bypass. Triple the layer thickness: measured loss 5 W. Determine which model fits and predict loss with doubled thickness.
stages.reconstruct: A fit R=30/9=10/3 K/W, triple predicts 3 W. B main 6 W and bypass 3 W (R_b=10); triple 2+3=5 W fits. Double predicts 3+3=6 W. Independent test supports B, not unique unrestricted explanation.
stages.diagnose: Identify whether you inferred a unique network from the initial total power or forgot which model parameter changes with thickness.
stages.repair: Fit both stipulated models to the first observation, propagate each through the changed geometry, compare independent predictions, and qualify the accepted model.
stages.boundary_test: If the bypass resistance also triples with layer thickness, does the 5 W prediction survive?

core1b.fresh_task: At fixed ΔT=20 K a nominal 4 K/W slab with an unknown extra path loses 7 W. Model A uses a changed effective slab resistance proportional to thickness. Model B retains nominal R with a fixed bypass. Doubling thickness gives 4.5 W. Test both, infer the bypass if supported, then predict total loss when thickness is quadrupled.

stages.predict: Before fitting, predict whether a single altered-slab model or an extra-path model will better fit the doubled-thickness measurement.
stages.attempt: At fixed ΔT=20 K a nominal 4 K/W slab with an unknown extra path loses 7 W. Model A uses a changed effective slab resistance proportional to thickness. Model B retains nominal R with a fixed bypass. Doubling thickness gives 4.5 W. Test both, infer the bypass if supported, then predict total loss when thickness is quadrupled.
stages.reconstruct: A R_eff=20/7; doubled predicts 3.5 W. B slab 5 W plus bypass 2 W (10 K/W); double 2.5+2=4.5 W fits. Quadruple 1.25+2=3.25 W. Only these specified models compared.
stages.diagnose: Identify whether you inferred a unique network from the initial total power or forgot which model parameter changes with thickness.
stages.repair: Fit both stipulated models to the first observation, propagate each through the changed geometry, compare independent predictions, and qualify the accepted model.
stages.boundary_test: If a fourth trial instead gives 4 W at quadruple thickness, what would you conclude?
